title: Common Topology Constraints
text: Do not recommend current-mode or cascaded control unless current sensing is either available or explicitly added to the design assumptions.

title: Common Topology Constraints
text: Record whether the intended operating region includes CCM, DCM, weak-grid operation, or bidirectional flow because those conditions change which controller families remain robust.

title: Buck Cascaded Control Notes
text: Use cascaded current-inner and voltage-outer loops for buck converters that must handle aggressive load steps or tighter transient limits than a plain voltage loop can satisfy.

title: Buck Cascaded Control Notes
text: If repeated evaluation failures cite overshoot or settling time, promote the design from plain PI to cascaded control before continuing to increase gains.

title: Buck PI Strategy Notes
text: Use a single voltage-loop PI controller for buck converters when the plant is well damped and implementation simplicity matters. This is the default starting point for non-isolated buck regulation.

title: Buck PI Strategy Notes
text: Escalate to cascaded current-mode control when transient recovery is too slow, overshoot remains high after reasonable gain tuning, or output filtering needs stronger disturbance rejection.

title: Three-Phase Inverter dq Notes
text: For three-phase inverter control, use synchronous-frame dq current regulation with an outer voltage or power loop when the application is grid connected and does not explicitly require grid-forming behavior.

title: Three-Phase Inverter dq Notes
text: Keep the current loop active by default and pair it with inrush limiting when startup current or grid synchronization can stress the converter.

title: Three-Phase Inverter AHO-Based VOC Notes
text: Use an AHO-based virtual oscillator controller for three-phase inverter grid-forming operation when sinusoidal self-synchronizing behavior is desired and the requirement explicitly prefers oscillator-based regulation over VSG emulation.

title: Three-Phase Inverter AHO-Based VOC Notes
text: Keep an inner current-limiting or current-regulating layer active beneath the oscillator so load-step and startup stress do not rely on oscillator dynamics alone. The oscillator should create the voltage waveform, while the current layer enforces protection.

title: Three-Phase Inverter AHO-Based VOC Notes
text: AHO-based VOC can provide clean sinusoidal references and autonomous synchronization, but amplitude restoration, dispatchability, and current-limit interaction must be tuned carefully in weak-grid operation.

title: Three-Phase Inverter VSG Notes
text: Use a virtual synchronous generator strategy in weak-grid or grid-forming scenarios where inertial response and voltage support are more important than the simplest tracking structure.

title: Three-Phase Inverter VSG Notes
text: VSG improves weak-grid behavior but tuning is more sensitive than plain dq control, so current-loop coordination and conservative bandwidth separation are important.

title: PFC Current-Mode Notes
text: For boost PFC and rectifier applications, use a dual-loop structure with an inner current loop and slower outer voltage loop. Startup current limiting should be explicit rather than implied.

title: DAB Implementation Patterns
text: Generate the phase-shift command as a timer compare value, not a duty-cycle register. Phase-shift resolution must be fine enough for smooth power control — at least 10 bits over the 0-to-pi range. Coarse resolution causes quantization-induced oscillation.

title: DAB Implementation Patterns
text: For current-mode control of DAB, sense the transformer series inductor current (not the output current). The inductor current is the actual control-relevant signal. Use a current transformer or sense resistor in the primary path.

title: DAB Implementation Patterns
text: When the power reference crosses zero, the phase-shift command must cross zero smoothly. Implement anti-windup that resets the integrator when the phase-shift command crosses zero. A small dead-band around phi=0 prevents chattering.

title: Common Implementation Patterns
text: Whenever modulation saturation is possible, include anti-windup behavior explicitly in the controller design rather than assuming the PI structure alone is sufficient.

title: Common Implementation Patterns
text: Treat startup and precharge as part of control implementation. Soft-start ramps and active current limits should be separate choices, not hidden side effects.

title: AHO-Based VOC Implementation Notes
text: Represent the oscillator with explicit state variables and compute modulation or voltage references primarily from those oscillator states. Do not reduce VOC to a PI controller plus a small sinusoidal injection term.

title: AHO-Based VOC Implementation Notes
text: Initialize oscillator states to a finite amplitude and pair them with active current limiting during startup so the converter does not produce a large uncontrolled transient while the oscillator builds.

title: AHO-Based VOC Implementation Notes
text: Generate three-phase references from the oscillator state itself or from an internally generated oscillator angle. Avoid using a fully independent fixed-frequency output angle that bypasses the oscillator dynamics.

title: AHO-Based VOC Implementation Notes
text: Apply current limiting and modulation saturation as bounded nonlinear constraints around the oscillator-generated reference rather than replacing the oscillator with a pure magnitude PI loop.

title: PFC Implementation Patterns
text: The PFC has three distinct loops: (1) inner current loop (fastest, tracks sinusoidal reference), (2) outer voltage loop (slowest, regulates bulk capacitor), (3) feedforward of rectified line voltage. Current reference = voltage-loop output * rectified line voltage shape.

title: PFC Implementation Patterns
text: PFC inrush is severe because the bulk capacitor charges through the boost inductor with no current limit at startup. Use a pre-charge resistor (bypassed after startup) or ramp the current reference from zero. The current loop alone cannot prevent inrush.

title: PFC Implementation Patterns
text: The rectified line voltage shape must be sensed accurately for the current reference. Use a dedicated voltage divider and filter. If the line voltage sensor has offset or distortion, the input current will have the same distortion.

title: Resonant Converter Implementation Patterns
text: The controller output is a switching frequency command, not a duty cycle. Map the PI output to a frequency register or timer period. Ensure the frequency is bounded: f_min <= f_command <= f_max. f_min prevents entering the ZCS region; f_max prevents excessive switching losses.

title: Resonant Converter Implementation Patterns
text: Resonant converters require precise dead-time for ZVS. Dead time must be long enough for MOSFET output capacitance to charge/discharge but short enough to avoid body diode conduction. Typical: 50-200ns depending on MOSFET Coss.

title: Resonant Converter Implementation Patterns
text: Start at maximum frequency (minimum gain) and ramp down to the target frequency. This limits inrush current through the resonant tank. Do not step the frequency command directly to the target — the tank current can exceed device ratings.

title: Architecture Escalation Decision Guide
section: When to escalate from PI to cascaded
text: Escalate when: (a) single-loop PI fails overshoot specs at the required bandwidth, (b) the plant has significant current dynamics that a voltage loop cannot handle, (c) current limiting is required for protection. The cascaded structure lets the inner loop handle fast dynamics.

title: Architecture Escalation Decision Guide
section: When to escalate from voltage-mode to current-mode
text: Escalate when: (a) the plant has a variable duty-cycle-to-output gain (boost, buck-boost), (b) the plant needs cycle-by-cycle current limiting, (c) the single-loop response is inconsistent across operating points. Current-mode control linearizes the plant.

title: Architecture Escalation Decision Guide
text: Switch when: (a) the RHPZ or other fundamental plant limitation prevents meeting bandwidth specs, (b) the efficiency requirement cannot be met, (c) isolation is required but the current topology is non-isolated, (d) bidirectional power flow is required but the current topology is unidirectional.

title: Architecture Escalation Decision Guide
text: Rare, but consider when: (a) current sensing noise is too high and cannot be filtered without destabilizing the loop, (b) the plant is inherently first-order and current-mode adds complexity without benefit, (c) the application is very low power where sensing overhead is disproportionate.

title: Architecture Escalation Decision Guide
text: Vout < Vin? -> Buck family. Vout > Vin? -> Boost family. Both possible? -> Buck-boost or isolated. Need isolation? -> Flyback (<75W), forward (75-200W), half/full bridge (>200W). Need bidirectional? -> DAB. Need AC output? -> Inverter family. Need PFC? -> PFC family. Need three-level? -> NPC or T-type.

title: Boost Converter Revision Patterns
text: Boost overshoot under load step shows a characteristic initial dip (non-minimum-phase undershoot) before the output recovers. This is caused by the RHPZ. Fix: reduce voltage-loop crossover below RHPZ/4, increase inner current-loop bandwidth, or add input voltage feedforward.

title: Boost Converter Revision Patterns
text: Slow settling on a boost usually means the voltage-loop bandwidth is below the RHPZ limit but gains are still too conservative. Check if the RHPZ frequency is lower than expected — this happens at light load (high R_load) or near-maximum duty cycle. Consider load-current feedforward.

title: Boost Converter Revision Patterns
text: Boost output ripple is dominated by the capacitor ESR and the charging/discharging current during switch on-time. At high duty cycle, the diode conducts for a short fraction of the period, so the capacitor must supply the load for most of the cycle. Verify C and ESR before changing gains.

title: Boost Converter Revision Patterns
text: Boost efficiency is primarily a function of conduction losses (which increase with duty cycle) and diode forward voltage. From the control side: verify the operating point is not in deep DCM at light load. Consider synchronous rectification or interleaving.

title: Boost Converter Revision Patterns
text: If boost fails across multiple iterations with current-mode control and the RHPZ frequency is below the required bandwidth, the topology cannot meet the transient spec. Consider interleaved boost (reduces effective RHPZ), buck-boost, or a different topology family.

title: Buck-Boost Revision Patterns
text: In boost-mode operation (V_out > V_in), the buck-boost has an RHPZ identical to a boost converter. If overshoot occurs in this region, reduce voltage-loop crossover below f_RHPZ/4. In buck-mode (V_out < V_in), there is no RHPZ — overshoot is a pure gain/tuning issue.

title: Buck-Boost Revision Patterns
text: The buck-boost plant dynamics change significantly between buck and boost modes. If settling is slow near the buck-boost boundary (V_out ~ V_in), the controller must handle the transition. Cascaded current-mode with gain scheduling is the robust solution.

title: Buck-Boost Revision Patterns
text: At extreme duty cycles (very high or very low D), the inductor current ripple increases. Verify the inductor sizing is adequate for the worst-case operating point. Controller gain changes will not fix ripple from undersized passives.

title: Buck-Boost Revision Patterns
text: Buck-boost efficiency is inherently lower than buck or boost alone because the current path always includes both the switch and the diode (or synchronous rectifier). The controller cannot improve this — consider a different topology if efficiency is critical.

title: Buck-Boost Revision Patterns
text: If the buck-boost fails transient specs across the full operating range, the plant dynamics are too variable for a fixed-gain controller. Consider: (1) gain scheduling based on duty cycle, (2) cascaded current-mode, or (3) a different topology if the conversion ratio is always step-down or always step-up.

title: Buck Converter Revision Patterns
text: For a buck under a load step, the dominant overshoot mechanism is a slow voltage loop responding to the inductor current's inability to track the load demand. The right fix is usually to add an inner current loop (cascaded structure) rather than lowering the voltage-loop proportional gain — lowering Kp makes settling worse without reducing the underlying current-rise lag.

title: Buck Converter Revision Patterns
text: Startup overshoot on a buck is almost always an anti-windup or integrator-preload issue, not a gain issue. Verify that the voltage-loop integrator clamps when the duty saturates and that soft-start ramps the reference rather than stepping it. Reducing Ki blindly will slow steady-state recovery without fixing the startup spike.

title: Buck Converter Revision Patterns
text: If a buck settles slowly after a load step but is stable, the controller bandwidth is too low relative to the LC corner. Promote to cascaded current-mode so the inner loop handles the fast current dynamics and the outer voltage loop can run wider. A single PI rarely achieves the required bandwidth without overshoot on a buck with light damping.

title: Buck Converter Revision Patterns
text: Steady-state output ripple on a buck is set primarily by the output capacitor ESR and the inductor current ripple, not by the controller. Before changing gains, recheck L, C, and ESR. Controller actions: (a) move sample time so the regulator does not chase switching ripple, (b) add a low-pass on the voltage sense path, (c) lower the loop bandwidth so the controller stops modulating duty in response to ripple.

title: Buck Converter Revision Patterns
text: If the output shows period-doubling or oscillation near fsw/2, this is subharmonic instability from peak-current-mode control without sufficient slope compensation. Add artificial ramp with slope >= inductor downslope / 2. Do not try to fix this with voltage-loop gain changes — it is an architecture-level issue.

title: Buck Converter Revision Patterns
text: Buck efficiency at light load is dominated by switching and gate-drive losses. The controller-side levers are: enable pulse-skipping or DCM operation if the plant supports it, lower the switching frequency, or transition to a burst-mode operating region. Do not address light-load efficiency by retuning voltage-loop gains.

title: CLLC Resonant Converter Revision Patterns
text: CLLC has a symmetric tank (series L and C on both sides) with a steep gain curve near resonance. If overshoot occurs, move the operating point to the inductive side (f > f_r) where the gain is flatter. The gain curve nonlinearity is worse than LLC near resonance.

title: CLLC Resonant Converter Revision Patterns
text: CLLC is designed for bidirectional power flow. If settling is slow during direction reversal, the frequency must sweep through the resonant point. Ensure the control can handle the zero-crossing of power without losing ZVS on both sides.

title: CLLC Resonant Converter Revision Patterns
text: Like LLC, the CLLC gain curve flattens at light load. If regulation fails at light load, consider burst mode or a wider frequency range. The symmetric tank means both sides have the same resonance — the gain curve shape is identical in both directions.

title: CLLC Resonant Converter Revision Patterns
text: If the CLLC cannot meet specs, the symmetric tank may need asymmetric redesign — different L_r/C_r values on primary and secondary. This breaks the symmetry but allows optimizing for a specific power direction.

title: Cuk Converter Revision Patterns
text: Cuk overshoot in CCM is the same mechanism as boost — the RHPZ limits voltage-loop bandwidth. Reduce kp to bring crossover below f_RHPZ/4. If the output is inverted, verify the feedback polarity is correct (negative feedback, not positive).

title: Cuk Converter Revision Patterns
text: If the Cuk settles slowly and gains are conservative, check the RHPZ frequency: f_RHPZ = (1-D)^2*R/(2*pi*L2). At high D and light load, this can be very low. Consider DCM operation or a different topology.

title: Cuk Converter Revision Patterns
text: The coupling capacitor C1 carries the full input+output ripple current. Its ESR directly affects output ripple. Increase C1 or use a lower-ESR type (film or ceramic). Controller gain changes will not fix ripple dominated by passive component sizing.

title: Cuk Converter Revision Patterns
text: If the Cuk shows period-doubling near fsw/2, this is subharmonic instability from peak-current-mode control. Add slope compensation with ramp >= (V_out)*D/(L2*fsw). This is an architecture fix, not a tuning fix.

title: Cuk Converter Revision Patterns
text: If the Cuk fails across iterations due to RHPZ limitation or the inverted output creates control complexity, consider SEPIC (non-inverted output, same RHPZ behavior) or flyback (if isolation is needed).

title: DAB Converter Revision Patterns
text: DAB overshoot is caused by the phase-shift command overshooting the target. The power-phase-shift relationship is sinusoidal, so the plant gain varies with operating point. Reduce kp or add nonlinear gain compensation that normalizes the gain variation.

title: DAB Converter Revision Patterns
text: DAB slow settling near zero power transfer is expected because the plant gain (dP/dphi) is near zero at phi=0. This is inherent to the topology. If the application requires fast regulation near zero power, consider adding a small bias phase shift.

title: DAB Converter Revision Patterns
text: DAB output ripple is determined by the inductor current ripple and the output capacitor. At high phase shift, the current waveform becomes more triangular. Verify the output capacitor sizing before changing gains.

title: DAB Converter Revision Patterns
text: DAB efficiency at light load is poor with SPS control due to circulating current. Switch to EPS or TPS modulation to reduce circulating current. This is an architecture-level change, not a tuning fix.

title: DAB Converter Revision Patterns
text: If DAB fails across iterations, consider the modulation scheme (SPS vs EPS vs TPS) and whether ZVS is being maintained. If ZVS is lost at the operating point, the topology may need a different modulation strategy or a wider series inductance.

title: Systematic Debugging Methodology for Power Converter Controllers
text: When a converter fails evaluation, diagnose in this order: (1) Implementation — verify sign, scale, wiring, and that the controller output reaches the plant. (2) Plant model — verify the topology template matches the controller. (3) Architecture — verify the control structure matches the plant. (4) Tuning — only after the above three are confirmed.

title: Systematic Debugging Methodology for Power Converter Controllers
section: When output is zero or near-zero
text: If the output never approaches the target, this is an implementation issue, not a tuning issue. Check: sensor polarity, controller output polarity, duty-cycle command range, and that the plant template is correctly wired. Do not waste iterations tuning gains.

title: Systematic Debugging Methodology for Power Converter Controllers
text: Oscillations have characteristic frequencies. Near fsw/2: subharmonic instability (add slope compensation). Near the LC resonance: insufficient damping (add active damping or reduce kp). Below fsw/10: integrator windup (add anti-windup). Very low frequency: limit cycle from saturation.

title: Systematic Debugging Methodology for Power Converter Controllers
section: When output overshoots and recovers slowly
text: Overshoot with slow recovery indicates the controller bandwidth is too low for the disturbance. The fix is usually to add an inner current loop (cascaded structure) rather than increasing the voltage-loop gains. Raising gains alone often makes the overshoot worse.

title: Systematic Debugging Methodology for Power Converter Controllers
text: If increasing or decreasing gains does not improve the failing metric, the sensitivity probe should detect this. The correct response is to switch architecture, not to keep trying different gain values. The plant may have a fundamental limitation (RHPZ, resonance, gain curve flatness).

title: Systematic Debugging Methodology for Power Converter Controllers
section: When the same failure repeats across 3+ iterations
text: This is the stagnation threshold. The system has tried multiple gain sets and possibly multiple architectures. Remaining possibilities: (1) plant model mismatch (wrong topology template), (2) missing sensor or control loop, (3) fundamental specification incompatibility with the chosen topology.

title: Flyback Converter Revision Patterns
text: Flyback overshoot often traces to insufficient slope compensation causing subharmonic instability (misread as tuning overshoot) or to the RHPZ limiting bandwidth in CCM. Verify slope compensation first, then check the RHPZ frequency at the operating point.

title: Flyback Converter Revision Patterns
section: Slow settling in DCM vs CCM
text: Flyback slow settling in DCM is usually acceptable (the plant is inherently slower in DCM). In CCM, check if the RHPZ is capping bandwidth below requirements. If so, this is a topology limitation — consider forward or half-bridge for higher power.

title: Flyback Converter Revision Patterns
text: Flyback output ripple has two components: (1) capacitor ESR ripple proportional to the output current, and (2) ripple from the discontinuous secondary current waveform. Verify C and ESR sizing before changing gains. The discontinuous current makes the ripple higher than a buck.

title: Flyback Converter Revision Patterns
section: Efficiency from leakage and magnetizing current
text: Flyback efficiency is dominated by the leakage inductance energy (requires snubber/clamp) and the transformer magnetizing current (circulating energy). The controller cannot improve these — they are plant design issues. Consider synchronous rectification.

title: Flyback Converter Revision Patterns
text: If flyback fails across iterations, consider: (1) switching from PSR to SSR feedback for better regulation, (2) switching from flyback to forward (for >50W), (3) adding synchronous rectification for efficiency.

title: Forward Converter Revision Patterns
text: Forward converter overshoot: the voltage loop is too slow for the load step. Switch to peak-current-mode for faster response. If already on current-mode, reduce the voltage-loop kp and increase ki for faster recovery without overshoot.

title: Forward Converter Revision Patterns
text: If the forward converter settles slowly, check the transformer reset. D must stay below 0.5 for volt-second balance with a reset winding. If the duty cycle is near 0.5, the reset time is minimal and the transformer may not fully reset — this causes rising magnetizing current and eventual saturation.

title: Forward Converter Revision Patterns
text: Output ripple is set by the output inductor current ripple and capacitor ESR. The forward converter has the same output stage as a buck. Recheck L, C, and ESR before changing gains.

title: Forward Converter Revision Patterns
text: Period-doubling near fsw/2 is subharmonic instability from peak-current-mode without slope compensation. Add ramp >= V_out/(N*L_out*fsw). This is an architecture fix, not a tuning fix.

title: Forward Converter Revision Patterns
text: If the forward converter cannot meet specs, consider: (1) two-switch forward for higher power and better reset, (2) push-pull or half-bridge for higher power, (3) flyback for simpler isolated design at lower power.

title: Full-Bridge Isolated Revision Patterns
text: Full-bridge overshoot: same as other isolated topologies — the voltage loop is too slow. With phase-shift modulation, the effective duty cycle changes nonlinearly with phase shift. Use peak-current-mode control for linearizing the power transfer.

title: Full-Bridge Isolated Revision Patterns
text: If the full-bridge settles slowly, check: (1) Is the phase-shift range adequate? At light load, the minimum phase shift may be too large, causing over-regulation. (2) Is the current loop fast enough? f_ci ~ fsw/5.

title: Full-Bridge Isolated Revision Patterns
text: Leakage inductance causes ringing on the primary during switching transitions. Add snubbers or use the parasitic ringing for ZVS (phase-shift full-bridge). Output ripple is set by the output inductor and capacitor — recheck passives.

title: Full-Bridge Isolated Revision Patterns
text: Phase-shift full-bridge loses ZVS at light load because the energy stored in the leakage inductance is insufficient to charge/discharge the MOSFET capacitances. The body diode conduction increases losses. Consider adaptive dead-time or burst mode at light load.

title: Full-Bridge Isolated Revision Patterns
text: If the full-bridge fails across iterations, consider: (1) PSFB (phase-shifted full-bridge) for better ZVS range, (2) resonant transition for wider ZVS, (3) LLC if the conversion ratio is fixed.

title: Half-Bridge Revision Patterns
text: Half-bridge overshoot: same as push-pull — the voltage loop is too slow. Switch to peak-current-mode if not already. The split-capacitor midpoint drifts under load step, adding a transient disturbance that the voltage loop must handle.

title: Half-Bridge Revision Patterns
text: Check: (1) current loop bandwidth f_ci ~ fsw/5, (2) slope compensation not excessive, (3) split-capacitor midpoint recovery. The midpoint drift creates an effective input voltage disturbance that slows settling.

title: Half-Bridge Revision Patterns
text: Leakage inductance ring with MOSFET Coss causes high-frequency oscillation on the primary. Add RCD snubbers. On the secondary, verify the output capacitor ESR is low enough for the ripple spec.

title: Half-Bridge Revision Patterns
text: If the split-capacitor midpoint drifts >5% from V_in/2, the transformer gets a DC bias. Causes: asymmetric gate drive, unequal blanking times, or unbalanced current sensing. Verify per-switch current sensing and symmetric layout.

title: Half-Bridge Revision Patterns
text: If the half-bridge cannot handle the power level (>1kW) or the voltage stress exceeds switch ratings, upgrade to full-bridge. Full-bridge uses all four quadrant switches and can deliver twice the power at the same switch stress.

title: Single-Phase Inverter Revision Patterns
text: Dead-time causes voltage distortion that is worst at low modulation index. Add dead-time compensation (feedforward voltage offset proportional to the sign of the output current). If THD still fails, increase the LC filter size or switching frequency.

title: Single-Phase Inverter Revision Patterns
text: Single-phase inverter overshoot under load step: the voltage loop is too slow. Increase kp. If using PR (proportional-resonant) controller, increase the resonant gain at the fundamental frequency. Add current limiting to prevent overcurrent during transients.

title: Single-Phase Inverter Revision Patterns
text: If the inverter settles slowly after a load step, the LC filter resonance may be under-damped. Add virtual resistance (active damping) via capacitor-current feedback. The damping gain: R_d ~ 1/(3*Cf*omega_res).

title: Single-Phase Inverter Revision Patterns
text: If the output frequency drifts, the PLL or oscillator reference is unstable. For standalone operation, use a crystal oscillator. For grid-tied operation, verify the PLL bandwidth is adequate (5-10x below the current-loop bandwidth).

title: Three-Phase Inverter Revision Patterns
text: Voltage overshoot under weak-grid conditions on a grid-forming inverter is usually a coupling problem between the inverter output impedance and the grid impedance, not a gain issue. Lowering controller gains often makes the inverter unstable instead. Prefer adding virtual impedance or active damping, or switching to a grid-forming architecture (VOC, VSG) if grid-following dq is the current choice.

title: Three-Phase Inverter Revision Patterns
text: Overshoot during a phase or frequency jump on a 3-phase inverter is a PLL/synchronization issue. Verify the PLL bandwidth is below the voltage-loop bandwidth by at least 3x. For grid-forming designs, ensure the oscillator angle is the reference of record and is not being snapped to a measured grid angle during the transient.

title: Three-Phase Inverter Revision Patterns
text: Slow settling on a 3-phase inverter usually traces to the LCL filter's lightly damped resonance, not the controller gains. Add active damping (capacitor-current feedback or virtual resistor) before tightening loop bandwidth. If active damping is present, verify the damping coefficient is matched to the LCL resonant frequency and the sampling rate.

title: Three-Phase Inverter Revision Patterns
text: If a dq-frame inverter settles slowly on a current reference step, check feedforward decoupling between d and q axes. Without ωL cross-decoupling, the two loops fight each other and effective settling time degrades. Adding decoupling is far more effective than raising loop gain.

title: Three-Phase Inverter Revision Patterns
text: Ripple at switching frequency on a 3-phase inverter output is set by the LCL filter and modulation strategy, not the controller. Verify L1, L2, Cf design against the switching frequency and check whether the modulation (SVPWM vs SPWM) is generating expected harmonic content. Controller action: ensure the sample time avoids aliasing the switching ripple into the regulated band.

title: Three-Phase Inverter Revision Patterns
text: Sub-synchronous oscillation (below grid fundamental) in weak-grid operation is an unstable interaction between PLL and current loop, frequently misclassified as ripple. The fix is to reduce PLL bandwidth substantially or, if grid-forming, drop the PLL entirely and rely on the internal oscillator.

title: Three-Phase Inverter Revision Patterns
text: Inverter efficiency is dominated by switching losses at high fsw and conduction losses at high current. From the controller side, the only meaningful lever is reducing the modulation index requirement (so deadtime and switching events drop) — this usually means accepting larger LCL filter components. Loop tuning does not recover inverter efficiency.

title: Three-Phase Inverter Revision Patterns
text: If a grid-following dq design fails across multiple revision iterations under weak-grid conditions, the architecture is the wrong choice — grid-following loses stability margin as the grid SCR drops. Escalate to a grid-forming architecture (VOC, VSG) rather than continuing to retune the dq loops.

title: LCC Resonant Converter Revision Patterns
text: If the LCC oscillates or overshoots near the resonant frequency, the gain curve is very steep in this region — small frequency changes cause large output changes. Move the operating point to the inductive side (f > f_r) where the gain curve is flatter and more controllable.

title: LCC Resonant Converter Revision Patterns
text: At light load, the LCC gain curve becomes very flat — large frequency changes produce minimal output change. The controller output saturates trying to regulate. Consider burst mode at light load or a wider frequency range.

title: LCC Resonant Converter Revision Patterns
text: If the LCC cannot regulate across the required load range, the tank component values (L_r, C_r, C_p) may need redesign. The parallel capacitor C_p sets the gain at light load; the series components set the resonant frequency. Adjust L_r/C_r ratio to shift the gain curve.

title: LCC Resonant Converter Revision Patterns
text: If operating above resonance (inductive side), the LCC achieves ZVS. If operating below resonance (capacitive side), it achieves ZCS but may lose ZCS at light load. Verify the operating region matches the switching device type (MOSFETs prefer ZVS, IGBTs prefer ZCS).

title: LLC Resonant Converter Revision Patterns
text: LLC overshoot is usually caused by the frequency command overshooting the target operating point on the gain curve. The gain curve is steep near resonance, so a small frequency overshoot causes a large voltage overshoot. Reduce kp or add a rate limiter on the frequency command.

title: LLC Resonant Converter Revision Patterns
text: LLC slow settling at light load is common because the gain curve is flat. This is a plant limitation, not a tuning problem. If the specification requires fast settling at light load, the tank design may need to change (lower Lm to increase the gain slope).

title: LLC Resonant Converter Revision Patterns
text: Output ripple on an LLC is dominated by the output capacitor ESR and the secondary-side current waveform. At the resonant frequency, the current waveform is nearly sinusoidal, which gives low ripple. If ripple is high, check whether the operating point is near the ZCS boundary.

title: LLC Resonant Converter Revision Patterns
text: LLC efficiency is dominated by conduction losses in the resonant tank and transformer. Verify the magnetizing current is not excessive (increases circulating energy). Operating closer to fr reduces circulating current but limits the gain range.

title: LLC Resonant Converter Revision Patterns
text: If the LLC fails across multiple iterations, the most likely cause is a tank design mismatch — the Lr, Cr, and Lm values do not produce the required gain at the required load. This requires redesigning the resonant tank, not retuning the controller.

title: NPC Three-Level Revision Patterns
text: If the split DC-bus capacitors oscillate (V_neutral drifts from V_dc/2), reduce the balancing loop gain or increase the DC-bus capacitance. If the oscillation frequency is near the current-loop bandwidth, the balancing and current loops are interacting — decouple them by reducing balancing bandwidth.

title: NPC Three-Level Revision Patterns
text: If output current THD fails spec, check: (1) LCL filter resonance is between 10*f_grid and fsw/2, (2) active damping is enabled (capacitor-current feedback), (3) dead-time compensation is applied. Dead-time distortion is worse at low modulation index.

title: NPC Three-Level Revision Patterns
text: DC-bus overshoot under load step: the voltage loop is too slow or the anti-windup is not working. Reduce voltage-loop kp or add proper anti-windup on the current reference saturation. The three-level topology has more headroom than two-level but the voltage loop design is the same.

title: NPC Three-Level Revision Patterns
text: If the DC bus settles slowly after a load step, the voltage-loop bandwidth is too low. Increase kp/ki, but keep f_cv < fsw/100. If the current loop is also slow, the dq decoupling may be incorrect — verify the decoupling terms use the actual filter inductance.

title: NPC Three-Level Revision Patterns
text: If the NPC cannot meet THD or efficiency specs, consider: (1) higher switching frequency (at the cost of switching losses), (2) T-type for lower voltage (<600V DC bus), (3) cascaded H-bridge for higher voltage (>3kV).

title: PFC Converter Revision Patterns
text: PFC overshoot on the bulk capacitor is a voltage-loop issue. The voltage-loop bandwidth must stay below 2*f_line (100 Hz for 50 Hz, 120 Hz for 60 Hz). If overshoot persists, add a notch filter at 2*f_line or reduce the voltage-loop bandwidth.

title: PFC Converter Revision Patterns
text: PFC settling is dominated by the voltage-loop bandwidth, which is intentionally low (10-20 Hz) to avoid distorting the current reference. This is by design. If faster settling is required, consider adding a fast inner voltage loop or accepting the slow response.

title: PFC Converter Revision Patterns
text: PFC output ripple at 2*f_line is inherent to single-phase PFC and cannot be eliminated by the controller. The ripple magnitude is: V_ripple = Pout/(2*pi*2*f_line*C_bulk). Reduce by increasing C_bulk. Controller gains cannot fix this.

title: PFC Converter Revision Patterns
text: PFC efficiency is dominated by the boost diode forward voltage and MOSFET switching/conduction losses. Consider totem-pole PFC with GaN/SiC for higher efficiency. The controller has limited ability to improve efficiency.

title: PFC Converter Revision Patterns
text: If PFC fails across iterations, verify the current reference is tracking the rectified sine waveform. If THD is high, increase current-loop bandwidth. If PF is low despite low THD, check the current-loop phase shift at the line frequency.

title: Totem-Pole PFC Revision Patterns
text: Totem-pole PFC current distortion near the AC zero crossing is caused by: (1) dead-time between the fast-path and slow-path switches, (2) inductor current discontinuity in CRM/DCM, (3) insufficient current-loop bandwidth. Increase current-loop crossover or use interleaved modulation.

title: Totem-Pole PFC Revision Patterns
text: The PFC output has inherent 2*f_line ripple from the power pulsation. The voltage-loop bandwidth MUST be below 2*f_line (~120Hz for 60Hz, ~100Hz for 50Hz) to avoid current distortion. If the ripple is excessive, increase the output capacitance — do not raise the voltage-loop bandwidth.

title: Totem-Pole PFC Revision Patterns
text: PFC voltage-loop overshoot: the bandwidth is already very low (<20Hz typical). If overshoot occurs, the kp is too high for the slow plant. Reduce kp and increase ki for steady-state accuracy without overshoot.

title: Totem-Pole PFC Revision Patterns
text: Totem-pole PFC with GaN/SiC loses ZVS at light load because the inductor current is discontinuous. This is a topology limitation. Consider: (1) CRM operation with variable frequency, (2) adaptive dead-time, (3) burst mode at light load.

title: Totem-Pole PFC Revision Patterns
text: If the totem-pole PFC cannot meet THD or efficiency specs, consider: (1) interleaved PFC for lower current ripple, (2) Vienna rectifier for three-phase applications, (3) conventional boost PFC with bridge rectifier if GaN/SiC is not available.

title: Phase-Shifted Full-Bridge Revision Patterns
text: PSFB has inherent duty-cycle loss due to the leakage inductance commutation time. This reduces the effective duty cycle and requires a higher turns ratio. If overshoot occurs, verify the turns ratio accounts for duty-cycle loss. The voltage loop should be designed for the effective duty cycle, not the nominal.

title: Phase-Shifted Full-Bridge Revision Patterns
text: If the PSFB loses ZVS (audible ringing on the primary), the switching losses increase and the effective gain changes. At light load, ZVS is lost — consider adaptive dead-time or burst mode. The current loop must handle the gain change from ZVS to hard-switching.

title: Phase-Shifted Full-Bridge Revision Patterns
text: The secondary rectifier ringing (from leakage inductance + junction capacitance) can couple to the output. Add RC snubbers across the secondary rectifiers. The output LC filter should be sized for the effective ripple frequency (2*fsw).

title: Phase-Shifted Full-Bridge Revision Patterns
text: PSFB efficiency at light load suffers from circulating current in the primary leg during the freewheeling interval. The controller cannot fix this — it is a topology limitation. Consider burst mode or a different topology for high efficiency across the full load range.

title: Phase-Shifted Full-Bridge Revision Patterns
text: If the PSFB cannot meet specs across the full load range, consider: (1) LLC for fixed conversion ratio with wide ZVS, (2) full-bridge with active clamp for better ZVS, (3) DAB for bidirectional power flow.

title: Push-Pull Revision Patterns
text: Push-pull overshoot is usually from a slow voltage loop that cannot handle the load step fast enough. If using voltage-mode control, switch to peak-current-mode for faster response and inherent flux balancing.

title: Push-Pull Revision Patterns
text: If the push-pull settles slowly, check: (1) Is the current loop fast enough? f_ci should be fsw/5 or higher. (2) Is slope compensation too aggressive? Excessive ramp reduces the current-loop gain. (3) Is the transformer saturating from flux imbalance?

title: Push-Pull Revision Patterns
text: Push-pull output ripple can be dominated by the leakage-inductance ring with MOSFET output capacitance. Add an RCD snubber across each primary half-winding. The snubber voltage should be 2-3x V_in.

title: Push-Pull Revision Patterns
text: Push-pull efficiency is dominated by transformer copper/core losses and switch conduction losses. The controller cannot improve efficiency. Consider: better core material, larger wire gauge, synchronous rectification on the secondary.

title: Push-Pull Revision Patterns
text: If the push-pull shows core saturation (rising current, collapsing output), the flux balance is broken. Verify: per-switch current sensing, symmetric gate drive, D<0.5. If flux imbalance persists, add a small air gap to the transformer core or use current-mode control with per-switch sensing.

title: Resonant Converter Revision Patterns
text: Resonant converter overshoot is caused by the steep gain curve near resonance. A small frequency overshoot near the resonant point causes a large gain change. Reduce kp or add a rate limiter on the frequency command.

title: Resonant Converter Revision Patterns
section: Slow settling from flat gain at light load
text: Resonant converters at light load have inherently flat gain curves, making the plant gain very low. This is a plant limitation. Gain scheduling by load current can help. If the specification requires fast settling at light load, the tank design may need to change.

title: Resonant Converter Revision Patterns
text: Resonant converter ripple is determined by the tank Q and the output capacitor. At resonance, the current waveform is nearly sinusoidal. If ripple is high, check whether operating near the ZCS boundary where diode reverse recovery causes high-frequency ringing.

title: Resonant Converter Revision Patterns
text: Resonant converter efficiency is dominated by circulating energy in the tank. Operating closer to fr reduces circulating energy but narrows the regulation range. The magnetizing current should be minimized while maintaining ZVS.

title: Resonant Converter Revision Patterns
text: If resonant converter fails across iterations, the tank parameters (Lr, Cr, Lm) are likely mismatched to the requirements. This requires redesigning the resonant tank, not retuning the controller. The gain curve must cover the required input voltage range at all loads.

title: Cross-Topology Revision Patterns
text: When overshoot remains high after reasonable gain reduction, prefer adding an inner current loop, feedforward, or saturation management before forcing more integral action.

title: Cross-Topology Revision Patterns
text: When settling time repeatedly fails, first check whether the control structure is too simple for the plant. A loop-structure change is often better than uniformly increasing gains.

title: Cross-Topology Revision Patterns
text: When ripple violations persist, examine passive sizing and switching ripple paths first; controller gain changes alone rarely remove steady ripple limitations.

title: Cross-Topology Revision Patterns
text: Efficiency shortfalls are mostly a plant-side problem, not a controller-tuning problem. Before adjusting gains, check whether the operating point sits in a high-conduction-loss region (heavy load, low Vin) or a high-switching-loss region (light load, high fsw). Controller-side responses are limited to: (1) lower switching frequency if the plant allows, (2) enable synchronous rectification if available, (3) reduce circulating current set by the current loop reference. Do not raise loop bandwidth to chase efficiency.

title: Cross-Topology Revision Patterns
text: If efficiency is failing together with the controller pegging the duty rail, the plant is undersized or the input voltage is outside the assumed range. Re-check the requirements before tuning further — no controller change recovers efficiency once the converter is in duty-cycle saturation.

title: Cross-Topology Revision Patterns
text: When several revision iterations on the same controller architecture fail to improve the score, the dominant failure mode is almost always an architecture mismatch, not a gain choice. Escalate by switching architecture (e.g. PI to cascaded current-mode, single-loop to multi-loop, linear to resonant for AC tracking), not by tightening the current architecture further.

title: Cross-Topology Revision Patterns
text: If the same diagnosis category repeats across 3 or more iterations with no score improvement, stop revising gains and instead question the plant model and sensor set. Common silent causes: missing current sensor that the chosen architecture assumes, sample time aliased to a plant resonance, unmodelled delay in the simulation harness, or saturation/anti-windup absent from the implementation.

title: SEPIC Revision Patterns
text: SEPIC overshoot in CCM is caused by the RHPZ limiting the voltage-loop bandwidth. If the crossover is above f_RHPZ/4, the phase margin collapses. Reduce kp until the crossover is below f_RHPZ/4, or switch to DCM operation which eliminates the RHPZ.

title: SEPIC Revision Patterns
text: If the SEPIC settles slowly and gains are already conservative, the RHPZ frequency at the operating point may be very low (high D, light load). Check f_RHPZ = R*(1-D)^2/(2*pi*L1). If f_RHPZ < 10*f_required, the topology cannot meet the spec in CCM.

title: SEPIC Revision Patterns
text: SEPIC output ripple depends on the coupling capacitor C1 and output capacitor ESR. The coupling capacitor carries high RMS current. If ripple is excessive, increase C1 or reduce its ESR before changing controller gains.

title: SEPIC Revision Patterns
text: SEPIC efficiency is limited by the coupled-inductor losses (winding and core) and the coupling capacitor RMS current. The controller cannot improve efficiency — it is a plant-side issue. Consider reducing coupling capacitor ESR or using a better inductor core material.

title: SEPIC Revision Patterns
text: If the SEPIC fails across multiple iterations with the RHPZ below required bandwidth, switch to DCM operation or consider a different topology (buck-boost for non-isolated, flyback for isolated).

title: Series Resonant Converter Revision Patterns
text: The SRC (series resonant converter) has a maximum voltage gain of 1 — it cannot step up the voltage. If the output cannot reach the target, verify the turns ratio is sufficient. The SRC is fundamentally limited to V_out <= V_in*N_sec/N_pri.

title: Series Resonant Converter Revision Patterns
text: At very light load, the SRC gain curve becomes extremely flat near resonance. The converter cannot regulate because large frequency changes produce negligible output change. This is a fundamental SRC limitation — consider LLC or LCC which have better light-load regulation.

title: Series Resonant Converter Revision Patterns
text: If the SRC shows oscillation at sub-harmonics of the switching frequency, the operating point may have jumped to the capacitive side (below resonance). Ensure the control always operates on the inductive side (f > f_r) for ZVS and stability.

title: Series Resonant Converter Revision Patterns
text: If the SRC cannot regulate across the required load range, upgrade to LLC (adds parallel inductor for better gain range) or LCC (adds parallel capacitor for high-voltage applications). The SRC is best suited for applications with narrow load range and V_out < V_in*N.

title: T-Type Three-Level Revision Patterns
text: Same as NPC: reduce balancing loop gain or increase DC-bus capacitance. The T-type bidirectional switches carry more current during zero-level, so thermal stress can cause asymmetric behavior if the switches are overheating.

title: T-Type Three-Level Revision Patterns
text: Same as NPC: check LCL filter resonance, active damping, dead-time compensation. T-type has slightly different harmonic distortion pattern because the zero-level path has different impedance than NPC.

title: T-Type Three-Level Revision Patterns
text: Same as NPC: reduce voltage-loop kp or fix anti-windup. The voltage-loop design is identical to NPC — the three-level structure does not change the voltage-loop dynamics.

title: T-Type Three-Level Revision Patterns
text: T-type efficiency is dominated by the bidirectional switch conduction losses during zero-level. At high DC-bus voltage (>600V), the bidirectional switches must be higher-voltage-rated with higher conduction loss. Consider switching to NPC topology.

title: T-Type Three-Level Revision Patterns
text: If the T-type cannot meet specs at the required voltage level, consider NPC (better at >600V) or two-level with higher switching frequency (simpler but higher THD). For very high voltage, cascaded H-bridge is the standard choice.

title: Vienna Rectifier Revision Patterns
text: Vienna rectifier current distortion is caused by: (1) incorrect space-vector modulation at the sector boundaries, (2) insufficient current-loop bandwidth, (3) neutral-point voltage oscillation. Check the modulation algorithm and increase current-loop crossover if below fsw/10.

title: Vienna Rectifier Revision Patterns
text: The split DC-bus capacitors develop a voltage imbalance. Add a balancing loop that adjusts the modulation to equalize the capacitor voltages. Bandwidth ~ f_ci/10. If oscillation persists, increase the DC-bus capacitance.

title: Vienna Rectifier Revision Patterns
text: If the DC bus settles slowly after a load step, the voltage-loop bandwidth is too low. Increase kp/ki, but keep f_cv < 2*f_line to avoid current distortion. The Vienna rectifier voltage loop is inherently slow (same as all PFC topologies).

title: Vienna Rectifier Revision Patterns
text: If the Vienna rectifier cannot meet THD or power factor specs, consider: (1) higher switching frequency, (2) interleaved Vienna rectifier, (3) active front-end with full-bridge for bidirectional capability.

title: Basso Designing Control Loops Source Metadata
text: Practical compensator design for switching converters should start from measured or simulated Bode plots of the plant, not from idealized transfer functions. This is especially critical for converters with RHPZ or variable plant behavior across operating conditions.

title: Basso Designing Control Loops Source Metadata
section: Type II and Type III compensators
text: Use Type II (PI with lead) for converters with ESR zero cancellation needs. Use Type III (PID with two zeros) for converters requiring high bandwidth with double-pole plants like LC filters. Place zeros at or below the LC resonant frequency.

title: Benchmarking Nonlinear Oscillators for Grid-Forming Inverter Control
text: Nonlinear oscillator based grid-forming control should be described with explicit oscillator states, amplitude-limiting dynamics, and a clearly defined mapping from oscillator state to inverter voltage or modulation commands.

title: Benchmarking Nonlinear Oscillators for Grid-Forming Inverter Control
text: Oscillator-based grid-forming controllers need explicit coordination between oscillator dynamics and inner current limiting so transient stress is bounded during startup and load steps.

title: De Doncker DAB Converter Source Metadata
text: DAB power transfer is P = Vin*Vout*phi*(pi-|phi|)/(2*pi*L*fsw*N). Single-phase-shift is simplest but has high circulating current at light load. Extended-phase-shift or triple-phase-shift adds degrees of freedom for ZVS maintenance and efficiency optimization.

title: De Doncker DAB Converter Source Metadata
text: ZVS is maintained when the transformer current reverses polarity during dead time. At light load or small phase shift, the current magnitude is insufficient to charge/discharge the MOSFET output capacitances, and ZVS is lost. This is the fundamental limitation of SPS control.

title: Erickson and Maksimovic Fundamentals Source Metadata
text: Boost converter voltage-loop bandwidth should respect the right-half-plane-zero limitation, which motivates cascaded or current-mode structures for stronger transient performance.

title: Kazimierczuk PWM DC-DC Power Converters Source Metadata
text: Current-mode control transforms the plant from second-order to first-order by making the inductor current follow the control signal. Subharmonic instability above 50% duty cycle requires slope compensation with ramp slope >= inductor downslope / 2.

title: Kazimierczuk PWM DC-DC Power Converters Source Metadata
text: The CCM/DCM boundary occurs at a load current that depends on the inductor value, duty cycle, and switching frequency. Below the boundary, the plant transfer function changes from second-order to first-order, requiring different compensator design.

title: Kolar Vienna Rectifier Source Metadata
text: The Vienna rectifier is a unidirectional three-phase PWM boost rectifier with inherent three-level modulation. Current control is typically in dq frame. Neutral-point voltage balancing is an additional control requirement that adjusts the common-mode duty-cycle offset.

title: Kolar Vienna Rectifier Source Metadata
text: Vienna rectifier advantages: only three active switches (vs six in conventional bridge), inherent three-level modulation reduces input current THD, no shoot-through risk. Limitation: unidirectional power flow only (boost mode). Neutral-point balancing required for three-level operation.

title: Mohan Undeland Robbins Source Metadata
text: Wide-range converters and bidirectional stages benefit from explicit current regulation because the actuator direction and duty-ratio sensitivity vary strongly over the operating envelope.

title: Steigerwald Resonant Converter Design Source Metadata
text: LLC resonant converter gain is controlled by switching frequency relative to the tank resonant frequency. Maximum gain occurs near the series resonant frequency. Operating above resonance achieves ZVS for primary switches. The gain curve is nonlinear and load-dependent.

title: Steigerwald Resonant Converter Design Source Metadata
text: Series resonant (SRC): gain <= 1, load-dependent, narrow control range. Parallel resonant (PRC): wider control range but high circulating current at light load. LLC combines both: wide control range with ZVS capability across load.

title: Teodorescu Grid Converters Source Metadata
text: LCL-filtered grid converters require explicit damping considerations in control design, especially when digital delay is not negligible.

title: TI Current Mode Control Source Metadata
text: Current-mode control reduces compensation burden for flyback-style stages and is usually the more practical starting point than voltage mode.

title: Voltage-Sourced Converters in Power Systems
text: Voltage-sourced converters are most naturally modeled and controlled in the synchronous dq reference frame, which transforms AC quantities to DC for PI control. The dq decoupling terms (omega*L cross-coupling) are essential for independent axis control.

title: Voltage-Sourced Converters in Power Systems
text: NPC and T-type three-level converters reduce THD and switch voltage stress compared to two-level. NPC is preferred above 600V DC bus; T-type is more efficient below 600V due to lower conduction loss in the neutral-point switches.

title: Bidirectional DC-DC Converter Dual-Loop Strategy
text: For bidirectional DC-DC stages, use a current-regulating inner loop with supervisory voltage or power command generation so charging and discharging share one bounded actuator.

title: Bidirectional DC-DC Converter Dual-Loop Strategy
text: The control layer should carry current and direction limits explicitly because sign reversal during mode changes is a primary source of transient stress.

title: Boost Converter Average Current Mode Strategy
text: Use an inner current loop with a slower outer voltage loop for boost converters when transient performance must improve without pushing the voltage loop near the right-half-plane-zero limit. Average current mode is preferred over peak current mode for boost PFC and high-power boost because it provides better noise immunity and more predictable loop gain.

title: Boost Converter Average Current Mode Strategy
text: Voltage-loop crossover: f_c < f_RHPZ/4 where f_RHPZ = R_load*(1-D)^2/(2*pi*L). Inner current-loop crossover: f_ci ~ fsw/10. Duty cycle: D = 1 - Vin/Vout in CCM. Inductor ripple: delta_IL = Vin*D/(L*fsw). Output capacitor for load step: C > I_step/(2*pi*f_c*delta_V_max).

title: Boost Converter Average Current Mode Strategy
text: The boost RHPZ frequency drops with increasing load resistance and increasing duty cycle. At maximum Vin/Vout ratio (worst case), the RHPZ is at its lowest frequency. Always verify stability at this operating point, not just at nominal conditions.

title: Boost Converter Average Current Mode Strategy
text: If a plain voltage loop becomes sluggish or overshoots as gains rise, move to average-current-mode control. If current-mode still fails, check whether the RHPZ is limiting bandwidth below the requirement — if so, this is an architecture limit and the topology may need to change to interleaved boost or a non-boost structure.

title: Buck-Boost Converter Generalized Strategy
text: For buck-boost stages operating over a wide conversion ratio, prefer a cascaded current-inner and voltage-outer structure so duty-ratio nonlinearity is handled by a faster inner actuator.

title: Buck-Boost Converter Generalized Strategy
text: Keep current sensing explicit in the design because a voltage-only loop usually becomes fragile once the operating point spans both buck-like and boost-like regions.

title: Buck Converter Strategy
text: Buck is the simplest step-down converter. Prefer cascaded current-inner voltage-outer control. The inner loop regulates inductor current, providing fast current limiting and damping the LC resonance. Single-loop PI is feasible but gives slower transients.

title: Buck Converter Strategy
text: V_out = D*V_in. LC resonance: f_LC = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(L*C)). Current-loop crossover: f_ci ~ fsw/5 to fsw/10. Voltage-loop crossover: f_cv < f_LC/3 for adequate phase margin. Inductor current ripple: delta_I = (V_in - V_out)*D/(L*fsw).

title: Buck Converter Strategy
text: The buck has no RHPZ, so the voltage-loop bandwidth is limited only by the LC resonance and the switching frequency. The LC resonance peak must be damped — either by the current loop (cascaded) or by adding a zero in the voltage compensator (single-loop PI). ESR of the output capacitor dominates steady-state ripple.

title: Buck Converter Strategy
text: If the buck cannot meet transient specs with a single PI, promote to cascaded current-mode. If the cascaded buck still cannot meet specs, the limitation is passive sizing (L, C) or the switching frequency — not the controller.

title: CLLC Resonant Converter Strategy
text: Use CLLC for bidirectional isolated DC-DC conversion. CLLC is symmetric — both primary and secondary have series L and parallel C. This enables ZVS on both sides for forward and reverse power flow.

title: CLLC Resonant Converter Strategy
text: CLLC has resonant tanks on both sides of the transformer. For reverse power flow, the secondary-side switches must be actively controlled (not just diodes). The gain curve is symmetric for forward and reverse operation.

title: CLLC Resonant Converter Strategy
text: Frequency control same as LLC. For bidirectional operation, the controller must switch the active bridge roles when power flow reverses. The frequency command is the same for both directions; the phase relationship between bridges determines power direction.

title: Cuk Converter Strategy
text: Cuk converter produces an inverted output voltage. In CCM it has an RHPZ similar to boost. Prefer cascaded current-inner voltage-outer control. The inner loop can regulate either L1 (input) or L2 (output) current. Output current sensing for the inner loop gives faster transient response.

title: Cuk Converter Strategy
text: V_out = -D*V_in/(1-D). RHPZ: f_RHPZ = (1-D)^2*R/(2*pi*L2) when sensing L2 current. CCM/DCM boundary depends on both inductors. Coupling capacitor C1 voltage = V_in + V_out (in magnitude). Voltage-loop crossover: f_c < f_RHPZ/4.

title: Cuk Converter Strategy
text: The coupling capacitor C1 carries high RMS ripple current and must be rated for the full input+output voltage. The inverted output means the feedback reference must be negative (or the sense circuit must invert). The RHPZ limits bandwidth in CCM, especially at high duty cycle.

title: Cuk Converter Strategy
text: If the Cuk cannot meet transient specs in CCM due to RHPZ, consider: (1) DCM operation (eliminates RHPZ but increases ripple), (2) coupled-inductor design to reduce component count, or (3) flyback if isolation is needed.

title: DAB Phase-Shift Control Strategy
text: Use phase-shift control for DAB converters. The DAB uses two full bridges with a series inductance. Power transfer is controlled by the phase shift between primary and secondary bridges. Single-phase-shift (SPS) is simplest but has high circulating current at light load.

title: DAB Phase-Shift Control Strategy
text: Power transfer (SPS): P = Vin*Vout*phi*(pi-|phi|)/(2*pi*L*fsw*N) where phi is phase shift in radians. Maximum power at phi = pi/2. Negative phi reverses power flow. Extended-phase-shift (EPS) adds duty-cycle ratio to reduce circulating current.

title: DAB Phase-Shift Control Strategy
text: Outer voltage loop PI generates a phase-shift command. Inner dynamics are fast (one switching cycle delay). Phase-shift command bounded to [-pi, pi]. Anti-windup is critical because phase-shift saturates at the power limit.

title: DAB Phase-Shift Control Strategy
text: ZVS is maintained when the transformer current reverses polarity during dead time. At light load or small phase shift, ZVS is lost and switching losses increase dramatically. This is the main limitation of SPS control.

title: DAB Phase-Shift Control Strategy
text: If SPS control cannot maintain ZVS across the load range, switch to extended-phase-shift (EPS) or triple-phase-shift (TPS) modulation. These add degrees of freedom for ZVS maintenance at light load at the cost of more complex control.

title: Flyback Converter Primary-Side Strategy
text: For flyback converters, start with current-mode control. For low-power (<75W) isolated applications, the flyback is the default choice. Primary-side regulation (PSR) eliminates the optocoupler but limits transient response. Secondary-side feedback with optocoupler gives better regulation.

title: Flyback Converter Primary-Side Strategy
text: Turns ratio N = Np/Ns. CCM: Vout = Vin*D/(N*(1-D)). DCM: Vout = Vin*D*sqrt(R_load/(2*L_mag*fsw))/N. RHPZ in CCM: f_RHPZ = R_load*(1-D)^2/(2*pi*L_mag*D). Slope compensation: m_c >= (Vout*N+Vin)/(2*L_mag*fsw).

title: Flyback Converter Primary-Side Strategy
text: The CCM/DCM boundary occurs at I_load_boundary = (Vin-Vout*D)*D/(2*L_mag*fsw*N). Below this load, the plant changes from double-pole+RHPZ to single-pole. Design compensation for worst case (CCM at full load) and accept larger margins in DCM.

title: Flyback Converter Primary-Side Strategy
text: Leading-edge blanking on the current sense signal is mandatory for flyback to filter the leakage inductance spike at turn-on. Typical blanking time: 100-300ns depending on leakage. If the design spans CCM and DCM, document the intended operating region.

title: Flyback Converter Primary-Side Strategy
text: If flyback with PSR fails transient specs, escalate to secondary-side feedback with optocoupler. If current-mode still fails, the flyback topology itself may be the limit — consider forward or half-bridge for higher power.

title: Forward Converter Strategy
text: Use forward converter for 50-200W isolated applications. Transfers energy during switch on-time (unlike flyback which stores energy). Duty cycle limited to D < 0.5 for volt-second balance with reset winding. Turns ratio: Vout = Vin*D/N.

title: Forward Converter Strategy
text: Use current-mode control (peak or average) for better transient response. The inner current loop handles the inductor dynamics; the outer voltage loop regulates output. Slope compensation required for D > 0.5 (if using extended duty range).

title: Forward Converter Strategy
text: The transformer must handle unidirectional flux — add a reset winding or use active clamp. Without reset, the transformer saturates. The reset winding limits D to < 0.5. Active clamp allows D > 0.5 and improves efficiency.

title: Forward Converter Strategy
text: If forward converter fails transient specs, check: (1) Is the transformer properly reset? (2) Is slope compensation adequate for the duty range? (3) Is the current-loop bandwidth high enough? If all checks pass, consider full-bridge for higher power.

title: Full-Bridge Isolated Converter Strategy
text: Use full-bridge isolated converter for >200W applications. Four primary switches allow duty cycle > 0.5 and full bipolar excitation of the transformer. Vout = Vin*D/N. Most efficient use of the transformer at high power.

title: Full-Bridge Isolated Converter Strategy
text: Use current-mode control with peak or average sensing on the primary. For ZVS operation, use phase-shift control between the two legs (see PSFB). Without phase-shift, use conventional PWM with slope compensation.

title: Full-Bridge Isolated Converter Strategy
text: Four switches increase cost and complexity. Ensure dead-time between complementary switches to prevent shoot-through. Current sensing on the primary requires a current transformer or sense resistor in the primary path.

title: Full-Bridge Isolated Converter Strategy
text: If efficiency is below target, consider phase-shift control (PSFB) for ZVS on primary switches. This reduces switching losses significantly at the cost of some duty-cycle loss.

title: Half-Bridge Converter Strategy
text: Half-bridge uses two switches with a split-capacitor voltage divider to generate a bipolar drive voltage. Duty cycle must stay below 0.5 per switch. Peak-current-mode control is preferred for inherent volt-second balancing and overcurrent protection.

title: Half-Bridge Converter Strategy
text: V_out = D*V_in/(2*N) where N = N_sec/N_pri, D<0.5. The split capacitors must be sized to hold the midpoint voltage within a few percent of V_in/2 under load. Effective output frequency = 2*fsw. Dead time: 50-200ns to prevent shoot-through.

title: Half-Bridge Converter Strategy
text: The split-capacitor midpoint voltage drifts if the two capacitors are not well matched or if the duty cycles are asymmetric. This causes DC bias in the transformer. Current-mode control with per-switch sensing corrects this automatically. The voltage stress on each switch is V_in (not V_in/2).

title: Half-Bridge Converter Strategy
text: If the half-bridge shows capacitor midpoint drift, verify the current sensing is per-switch. If the switches are overstressed (V_in > switch rating), consider a full-bridge for higher voltage applications. For power > 1kW, full-bridge is typically more efficient.

title: Single-Phase Inverter PR Strategy
text: For single-phase inverter sinusoidal output regulation, a proportional-resonant controller is a practical default because it tracks the fundamental in stationary frame without dq transformation.

title: Single-Phase Inverter PR Strategy
text: Add explicit output-voltage feedback filtering and saturation-aware anti-windup so resonant gain does not amplify startup or load-step distortion.

title: Three-Phase LCL Grid-Tied Inverter Strategy
text: For a three-phase grid-tied inverter with an LCL filter, use dq current regulation with PLL-based synchronization and treat resonance damping as a first-class design requirement. The LCL resonance must be damped before pushing current-loop bandwidth.

title: Three-Phase LCL Grid-Tied Inverter Strategy
text: L1 (inverter side) sized for current ripple 10-25% of rated current at fsw. Cf sized so LCL resonance f_res = 1/(2*pi)*sqrt((L1+L2)/(L1*L2*Cf)) falls between 10*f_grid and fsw/2. L2 (grid side) typically 1/3 to 1/5 of L1.

title: Three-Phase LCL Grid-Tied Inverter Strategy
text: Capacitor-current feedback with gain R_d acts as virtual resistor in series with Cf. Starting point: R_d ~ 1/(3*Cf*omega_res). Without active damping, the LCL resonance appears as a sharp peak in the loop gain that destabilizes the current loop.

title: Three-Phase LCL Grid-Tied Inverter Strategy
text: PLL bandwidth should be 5-10x below the current-loop bandwidth. For current-loop crossover of fsw/10, set PLL crossover to fsw/100 or lower. In weak grid (SCR < 3), reduce PLL bandwidth further or switch to grid-forming control (VSG/VOC/droop).

title: Three-Phase LCL Grid-Tied Inverter Strategy
text: The d-axis and q-axis plants are coupled through omega*L cross-terms. Without feedforward decoupling (Vd_ff = -omega*L*Iq, Vq_ff = omega*L*Id), the loops fight each other and effective bandwidth drops by 50% or more.

title: Three-Level NPC Inverter Strategy
text: NPC (Neutral-Point Clamped) is a three-level inverter with four switches per leg. The dq-frame current controller decouples the d and q axes. An outer voltage loop regulates the DC bus. The neutral-point voltage must be actively balanced.

title: Three-Level NPC Inverter Strategy
text: The split DC-bus capacitors develop a voltage imbalance due to asymmetric switching. A balancing algorithm adjusts the dwell time of the inner voltage level (zero vector) to equalize the capacitor voltages. The balancing loop bandwidth should be ~1/10 of the current loop.

title: Three-Level NPC Inverter Strategy
text: Output voltage levels: +V_dc/2, 0, -V_dc/2. Line-to-line voltage has 5 levels. THD is lower than two-level for the same switching frequency. Current-loop crossover: fsw/10. Voltage-loop crossover: fsw/50 to fsw/100. LCL filter resonance: f_res between 10*f_grid and fsw/2.

title: Three-Level NPC Inverter Strategy
text: NPC requires careful dead-time management to avoid shoot-through and ensure proper zero-level clamping. The inner switches (S2, S3) have different switching loss profiles than the outer switches (S1, S4). Neutral-point balancing fails if the current unbalance exceeds the capacitor sizing margin.

title: Three-Level NPC Inverter Strategy
text: If neutral-point balancing oscillates, reduce the balancing loop gain or increase the DC bus capacitor size. If THD fails spec, check LCL filter resonance placement and active damping. For higher voltage (>1kV), consider T-type or cascaded H-bridge.

title: Three-Level T-Type Inverter Strategy
text: T-type is a three-level inverter with two main switches per leg (connected to DC+ and DC-) plus a bidirectional switch to the neutral point. It has lower conduction losses than NPC at lower voltage ratings. Same dq-frame control structure as NPC.

title: Three-Level T-Type Inverter Strategy
text: Same balancing algorithm as NPC: adjust dwell time at the zero voltage level to equalize split-capacitor voltages. The bidirectional neutral-point switch carries the balancing current — ensure its current rating is sufficient. Balancing loop bandwidth ~1/10 of current loop.

title: Three-Level T-Type Inverter Strategy
text: Output voltage levels: +V_dc/2, 0, -V_dc/2 (same as NPC). The main switches (S1, S4) see full DC bus voltage. The bidirectional switches (S2, S3) see half the DC bus voltage but carry the full output current during zero-level operation. Current-loop crossover: fsw/10.

title: Three-Level T-Type Inverter Strategy
text: T-type has higher efficiency than NPC below ~600V DC bus because the neutral-point switches have lower voltage rating and thus lower conduction loss. Above ~600V, NPC is preferred because the neutral-point switches must be rated for V_dc/2. Dead-time between main and bidirectional switches is critical.

title: Three-Level T-Type Inverter Strategy
text: Same as NPC: if neutral-point balancing oscillates, reduce gain or increase capacitor size. If efficiency is below spec, verify the bidirectional switch selection (SiC MOSFETs can improve efficiency at higher voltage). For voltage >1kV, NPC is structurally more appropriate.

title: LCC Resonant Converter Strategy
text: Use LCC for high-output-voltage applications where parasitic capacitance is significant. LCC uses a parallel capacitor instead of a parallel inductor (as in LLC). The parallel capacitor can absorb transformer parasitic capacitance.

title: LCC Resonant Converter Strategy
text: LCC has a parallel capacitor Cp instead of a parallel inductor Lm. The gain characteristics are similar to LLC but the parallel resonant frequency depends on Cp. LCC is preferred when the transformer secondary has significant parasitic capacitance.

title: LCC Resonant Converter Strategy
text: Same as LLC: PI controller with kp in Hz/V and ki in Hz/(V*s). Operate above the series resonant frequency for ZVS. The gain curve shape depends on the ratio of Cp to Cr.

title: LLC Resonant Converter Frequency Control Strategy
text: Use frequency control for LLC resonant converters. The LLC achieves ZVS for primary switches when operating above the series resonant frequency (fsw > fr). The control variable is switching frequency, NOT duty cycle. kp and ki are frequency-controller gains in Hz/V and Hz/(V*s).

title: LLC Resonant Converter Frequency Control Strategy
text: Series resonant frequency: fr = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(Lr*Cr)). Parallel resonant frequency: fp = 1/(2*pi*sqrt((Lr+Lm)*Cr)). Voltage gain: M = Vout/(Vin/2) for full-bridge, M = Vout/(Vin*N/2) for half-bridge. Frequency range: typically 0.8*fr to 1.5*fr.

title: LLC Resonant Converter Frequency Control Strategy
text: Below fr: ZVS region with high gain, limited by magnetizing current. Above fr: ZVS region with decreasing gain. Between fr and fp: ZCS region for secondary diodes — causes reverse recovery losses. Always operate above fp to avoid ZCS region.

title: LLC Resonant Converter Frequency Control Strategy
text: The LLC gain curve is nonlinear. At light load (high Q), the gain curve is flat and frequency must change a lot to regulate. At heavy load, the gain curve is steep and small frequency changes cause large voltage changes. Design the PI for the worst case (light load, minimum gain slope).

title: LLC Resonant Converter Frequency Control Strategy
text: If the LLC frequency range cannot cover the required input voltage range at the given load, the tank design (Lr, Cr, Lm) must be redesigned — this is not a tuning problem. If output ripple is too high, check whether the resonant tank Q is too low.

title: Boost PFC Strategy
text: Boost PFC is the standard single-phase power factor correction topology. A three-loop structure: inner current loop shapes the input current to follow the rectified line voltage, outer voltage loop regulates the DC bus, and a multiplier generates the current reference from the voltage error and the line voltage waveform.

title: Boost PFC Strategy
text: Current-loop crossover: f_ci ~ fsw/10. Voltage-loop crossover: f_cv < 2*f_line/10 (~10-20Hz for 50/60Hz). The voltage loop must be slow enough to avoid distorting the current reference. RHPZ: f_RHPZ = R_load*(1-D)^2/(2*pi*L). At high line and light load, f_RHPZ is lowest.

title: Boost PFC Strategy
text: The 2*f_line ripple on the DC bus is inherent. If the voltage-loop bandwidth is too high, this ripple modulates the current reference, causing input current distortion (cross-over distortion). The voltage-loop compensator must have low gain at 2*f_line. Output capacitor sizing: C_out >= P_out/(2*pi*f_line*V_ripple*V_out).

title: Boost PFC Strategy
text: At startup, the output capacitor charges through the boost diode with no current limiting. Add an inrush limiting circuit (NTC relay or pre-charge MOSFET) or ramp the voltage reference during startup. The current loop must be enabled before the voltage loop reaches regulation.

title: Boost PFC Strategy
text: If the PFC cannot meet THD or power factor specs: (1) increase current-loop bandwidth, (2) add feedforward of the line voltage, (3) consider interleaved PFC for lower current ripple. If efficiency is the issue, consider totem-pole PFC with GaN/SiC for bridgeless operation.

title: Totem-Pole PFC Strategy
text: Use totem-pole PFC for high-efficiency power factor correction. Replaces the bridge rectifier with active switches for near-zero conduction loss. Requires GaN or SiC MOSFETs for the fast-switching leg (line-frequency commutation).

title: Totem-Pole PFC Strategy
text: Same voltage/current dual-loop as conventional boost PFC: outer voltage loop (10-20 Hz bandwidth) generates current amplitude reference, inner current loop tracks the sinusoidal reference. The current reference is the voltage-loop output multiplied by the rectified line voltage shape.

title: Totem-Pole PFC Strategy
text: Dead-time management is critical for the fast-switching leg. At light load, ZVS may be lost on the fast-switching leg, causing reverse recovery losses in the body diode. The slow-switching leg operates at line frequency (50/60 Hz) and uses MOSFETs with low Rds_on.

title: Totem-Pole PFC Strategy
text: If totem-pole PFC efficiency is below target, check: (1) Is ZVS maintained on the fast-switching leg? (2) Is the dead-time optimized? (3) Are the GaN/SiC devices properly driven? Efficiency loss is usually a hardware issue, not a control issue.

title: Phase-Shifted Full Bridge Strategy
text: Use PSFB for 200W-5kW isolated applications requiring high efficiency. Phase-shift modulation between the two legs achieves ZVS on primary switches. Power transfer: Vout = Vin*(2*D-1)/N where D is the effective duty cycle of overlapping conduction.

title: Phase-Shifted Full Bridge Strategy
text: Use current-mode control with slope compensation for the extended duty range. The phase-shift between legs is the primary control variable. Current sensing on the primary with a current transformer or sense resistor.

title: Phase-Shifted Full Bridge Strategy
text: Duty-cycle loss: the effective duty cycle at the secondary is less than the primary due to the phase-shift overlap. ZVS is maintained by the transformer leakage inductance and MOSFET output capacitance. At light load, ZVS may be lost.

title: Phase-Shifted Full Bridge Strategy
text: If PSFB efficiency is below target at light load, ZVS is likely lost. Options: (1) add a saturable inductor to extend ZVS range, (2) use adaptive dead-time control, (3) accept the switching loss if the load range is narrow.

title: Push-Pull Converter Strategy
text: Push-pull uses two switches driving a center-tapped transformer. Duty cycle must stay below 0.5 to prevent simultaneous conduction. Peak-current-mode control is strongly preferred over voltage-mode to handle flux imbalance and provide automatic current sharing.

title: Push-Pull Converter Strategy
text: V_out = D*V_in*N_sec/N_pri (per half-cycle, D<0.5). Transformer turns ratio N = N_sec/N_pri sets the conversion ratio. Effective switching frequency at the output is 2*fsw. Reset volt-second = D*V_in/fsw per half-cycle.

title: Push-Pull Converter Strategy
text: Flux imbalance: even small duty-cycle asymmetry causes DC bias in the transformer core. Current-mode control with per-switch current sensing provides inherent flux balancing. Voltage-mode requires external flux-balance circuits. Add leading-edge blanking (100-300ns) to blank the MOSFET turn-on spike.

title: Push-Pull Converter Strategy
